title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
official_title: To amend title 11, United States Code, to modify certain bankruptcy eligibility requirements, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) with 5 cosponsors, this bill sets new debt limits for two bankruptcy tracks: $7.5M for Subchapter V small-business reorganization and $2.75M for Chapter 13 individual reorganization. The bill passed the Senate on August 3, 2026 and awaits House action. It is a narrow debt-limit adjustment within existing bankruptcy chapters (no new program authority and no appropriation) — a low-controversy structure for the House to take up.

referencedSources.label: 11 U.S.C. 1182 (Bankruptcy Code — Subchapter V debtor definitions)
11 U.S.C. 109 (Bankruptcy Code — Who may be a debtor)

summary: This bill rewrites two bankruptcy debt-limit rules in title 11 of the U.S. Code. First, it replaces the current definition of "debtor" in Section 1182(1) — the eligibility gate for Subchapter V small business reorganization under Chapter 11 — with a new definition covering a person engaged in commercial or business activities (with affiliates counted together and single-asset real estate excluded) that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts of not more than $7.5M (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders), at least 50 percent of which arose from commercial or business activities. It bars public reporting companies and their affiliates from Subchapter V and disallows any group of affiliated debtors whose combined qualifying debts exceed $7.5M. Second, it rewrites Section 109(e) so that only individuals with regular income (or such an individual and spouse, other than a stockbroker or commodity broker) with noncontingent liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2.75M are eligible to file under Chapter 13 — replacing the current split limits for secured and unsecured debt. The amendments apply to cases commenced on or after enactment.
brief: Rewrites Subchapter V small business bankruptcy eligibility to a single $7.5M combined-debt limit and Chapter 13 individual eligibility to a single $2.75M combined-debt limit, effective for cases filed on or after enactment.

top_lines.headline: Subchapter V Small Business Debt Limit
subs: New 11 U.S.C. §1182(1)(A) covers persons engaged in commercial/business activities (including affiliates that are also debtors) with aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts of not more than $7.5M (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders)
At least 50 percent of the debt must have arisen from the commercial or business activities of the debtor
Excludes single-asset real estate debtors whose primary activity is owning single-asset real estate

top_lines.headline: Subchapter V Group and Public-Company Exclusions
subs: Bars any member of a group of affiliated debtors whose aggregate qualifying debts exceed $7.5M (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders)
Bars any debtor that is a corporation subject to Section 13 or 15(d) reporting under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78m, 78o(d))
Bars any debtor that is an affiliate of such a public reporting company

top_lines.headline: Chapter 13 Individual Debt Limit
subs: New 11 U.S.C. §109(e): only an individual with regular income (or such an individual and spouse, other than a stockbroker or commodity broker) with noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2.75M is eligible to file under Chapter 13
Replaces the current version of §109(e), which splits its debt limit into a secured-debt cap and an unsecured-debt cap

top_lines.headline: Effective Date
subs: The amendments made by the Act apply to any case commenced under title 11, United States Code, on or after the date of enactment

sections.label: Section 2(a) — Subchapter V Small Business Debt Limit (11 U.S.C. §1182(1))

items.main: Rewrites the definition of "debtor" for Subchapter V of Chapter 11 (Small Business Debtor Reorganization).
items.detail: The new definition is set out as a two-part structure. Subparagraph (A) covers a person engaged in commercial or business activities (including any affiliate of such person that is also a debtor under title 11, and excluding a person whose primary activity is the business of owning single-asset real estate) that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts, as of the date of the filing of the petition or the date of the order for relief, of not more than $7.5M (excluding debts owed to one or more affiliates or insiders), not less than 50 percent of which arose from the commercial or business activities of the debtor.

items.main: Adds three Subchapter V exclusions in new §1182(1)(B).
items.detail: The new subparagraph excludes: (i) any member of a group of affiliated debtors under title 11 that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts greater than $7.5M (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders); (ii) any debtor that is a corporation subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. §78m, §78o(d)); and (iii) any debtor that is an affiliate of a corporation described in clause (ii).

sections.label: Section 2(b) — Chapter 13 Individual Debt Limit (11 U.S.C. §109(e))

items.main: Strikes and rewrites §109(e) so Chapter 13 eligibility is set by a single combined-debt cap.
items.detail: The new §109(e) provides: only an individual with regular income that owes, on the date of the filing of the petition, noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2.75M — or an individual with regular income and such individual's spouse, except a stockbroker or commodity broker, that owe, on the date of the filing of the petition, noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2.75M — may be a debtor under Chapter 13. Per the fetched text of the current 11 U.S.C. §109, this replaces a split limit that used a secured-debt cap and an unsecured-debt cap; the bill collapses that structure into a single aggregate-debt threshold.

items.main: Applies the amendments to any case commenced under title 11 on or after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Pending cases filed before enactment remain governed by prior law.

underreported.summary: The affiliated-group cap treats any member of an affiliated-debtor group whose combined qualifying debts exceed $7.5M as ineligible for Subchapter V — even if that member alone would qualify.
underreported.why_unreported: Coverage of Subchapter V threshold bills tends to focus on the headline dollar limit. The affiliated-group aggregation rule is the operative provision that determines how the limit applies to holding-company structures and franchisee networks.

underreported.summary: Public reporting companies (§13 or §15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act) and their affiliates are barred from Subchapter V.
underreported.why_unreported: The Subchapter V regime is generally understood to be for small businesses. Codifying a categorical exclusion for reporting companies and their affiliates puts a bright-line rule into statute that closes a workaround for public-company subsidiaries.

gaps: The bill sets a $7.5M debt cap for Subchapter V and a $2.75M debt cap for Chapter 13 but does not index either threshold to inflation, so real-terms limits will erode over time.
The bill excludes public reporting companies and their affiliates from Subchapter V but does not address privately-held companies whose beneficial owners are public reporting entities.
The bill replaces the split secured/unsecured Chapter 13 debt limit with a single aggregate cap but does not address how debts secured by a spouse's separate property are counted.
The bill applies only to cases commenced on or after enactment and does not offer transition relief for cases already dismissed on eligibility grounds under the prior thresholds.

added: New categorical exclusions from Subchapter V for members of affiliated-debtor groups over $7.5M, public reporting companies under §13 or §15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and affiliates of such reporting companies (new 11 U.S.C. §1182(1)(B))
modified: 11 U.S.C. §1182(1) — Definition of "debtor" for Subchapter V rewritten to a $7.5M combined-debt cap with a 50%-commercial-origin requirement
11 U.S.C. §109(e) — Chapter 13 eligibility rewritten to a single $2.75M aggregate noncontingent-liquidated-debt cap
